passage: In the Delhi flat, Dadi sat on the sofa. Lalremsiami knelt beside her daughter Kavitha, two, and bent her own head to Dadi's feet. "Like this, Kavi." Kavitha flopped forward, giggling, and patted Dadi's toes. Dadi laughed and put both hands on Kavitha's curls. "Jeeti raho!" Kavitha looked up, beaming, and did it again. And again. Each time, Dadi laughed.

qa.q: What did Kavitha pat?
qa.a: She patted Dadi's toes.

qa.q: How did Kavitha seem to feel when Dadi put her hands on her curls?
qa.a: Kavitha seemed happy and delighted, beaming and doing it again and again.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that helped Kavitha learn?
qa.a: She showed the gesture herself first and made it gentle and playful.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Kavitha keeps bending to her feet?
qa.a: Dadi probably feels full of affection and joy, laughing and blessing her every time.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler guided to bend to a grandparent's feet as a game, who links the gesture to smiles and blessing.

passage: The doorbell rang in the Chennai flat. "Francis, guests!" called Amma. Francis, five, ran to the door and pressed his palms together, the way Amma had shown him. "Vanakkam, Uma aunty!" Uma aunty bent down and patted his cheek. "Such a good boy. God bless you." Francis turned pink. He brought her a glass of water, walking very slowly so it wouldn't spill. Later, when more guests came, he stood at the door waiting, palms ready.

qa.q: What did Francis bring Uma aunty?
qa.a: A glass of water.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Uma aunty blessed him?
qa.a: He felt shy and pleased, turning pink.

qa.q: What does Amma's teaching do well?
qa.a: It gives Francis a simple greeting that brings him warmth from guests, so he wants to welcome more people.

qa.q: How might Uma aunty feel being greeted at the door by Francis?
qa.a: She probably feels welcomed and charmed by the little boy's greeting.

grounding: It illustrates a child greeting guests with folded hands and receiving blessings, growing a feeling of being welcomed into a bigger circle.

passage:
The wedding hall in Lucknow was full of shiny saris and loud music. "Ujjwal, touch Mamaji's feet. Now Bade Nanaji. Now that aunty." Mummy kept steering him by the shoulder. Ujjwal, ten, bent again and again. Some of these people he had never seen. By the twentieth person, Ujjwal's cheeks were burning. He hid behind a pillar.
Indu Bua found him there. "Tired of bending?" He nodded, eyes stinging. "I don't even know them." Bua sat on the steps beside him. "Touching feet is a way to show respect you feel. It isn't a punishment. For people you don't know, a namaste is fine." Ujjwal looked up. "Mummy will be angry." "I'll talk to her," Bua said. She did. After that, Ujjwal did namaste for strangers and touched Nanaji's feet properly, slowly, because he loved Nanaji.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal hide?
qa.a: Behind a pillar.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel by the twentieth person?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, his cheeks burning, bowing to people he didn't know.

qa.q: How did Indu Bua help Ujjwal?
qa.a: She explained that touching feet is voluntary respect, offered namaste as a choice for strangers, and spoke to Mummy for him.

qa.q: How might Mummy have seen her steering at the wedding?
qa.a: Mummy probably wanted Ujjwal to show good manners in front of the family and didn't notice how uneasy it made him.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to touch every relative's feet at a wedding who feels uneasy, and an adult who explains the gesture is voluntary respect.

passage:
Diwali night
Today I touched about fifteen people's feet. Honestly, most of them I did in two seconds, half-bent, eyes on my phone, because the cousins were waiting to burst crackers. Nani caught my hand after I did hers. "Are you touching my feet or the floor?" Everyone laughed. I laughed too, but I felt a bit ashamed.
Later I was texting Ayesha. She asked what touching feet actually means, because her family says salaam instead. I started typing "respect" and then stopped. If it's respect, why was I doing it like ticking boxes?
So after the crackers I went back to Nani, who was sitting alone with her tea. I touched her feet slowly this time, and looked at her face. She put her hand on my head for a long time and didn't say anything. Her eyes were wet. It felt completely different. I think it's only real when you actually see the person.
Yash

qa.q: What did Nani ask Yash?
qa.a: "Are you touching my feet or the floor?"

qa.q: How did Yash feel when Nani caught the hurried gesture?
qa.a: Yash felt a bit ashamed, even while laughing with everyone.

qa.q: What made the second time real?
qa.a: Doing it slowly and looking at Nani's face gave the gesture real attention, so it became respect rather than a ticked box.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt the second time?
qa.a: She probably felt deeply touched and loved, keeping her hand on Yash's head with wet eyes.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who questions whether touching feet is respect or habit, and finds it real when done with attention.

passage:
Sunday night
Verma uncle came for lunch again. Every time, he grabs me in a long hug that doesn't end, squeezes my cheeks and says, "Give uncle a kissie." I'm fourteen. I hate it. My stomach goes tight when I hear his car. Everyone laughs.
Today I stepped back and did namaste instead. He said, "Oho, too big for uncle now?" and pulled me in anyway. My face went hot. Minakshi masi saw my face. She came straight over and said, "Anand does namaste now, Vermaji. That's a lovely greeting." She put her hand on my shoulder and kept it there.
After he left, masi sat with me on the terrace. She said my discomfort is real and I don't owe anyone a hug or a kiss. Then she told Mummy, right then, before dinner. Mummy listened and said, "Next time you do namaste, and I'll stand with you." I felt like I could breathe.
Anand

qa.q: How old is Anand?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: How does Anand feel when Verma uncle arrives?
qa.a: Anand feels uncomfortable and tense, with a tight stomach, hating the long hugs and forced kisses.

qa.q: What did Minakshi masi do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She stepped in immediately, named namaste as a lovely greeting, believed Anand's discomfort and told Mummy the same evening, so Anand had adults on side.

qa.q: How might Verma uncle see his hugs?
qa.a: He probably sees them as affection and doesn't notice Anand's discomfort, which is why he laughed it off.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager uncomfortable with a relative's long hugs and forced kisses, whose discomfort is believed and namaste accepted as a choice.

passage:
Devika, twenty-one, had come to Tejas's village near Nashik for his sister's wedding, and she had no rule book. At the gate, Tejas's grandmother sat on a cot. Devika bent towards her feet; the old woman smiled and blessed her, pleased. Next came Tejas's uncle's friend, Jameel chacha, in a white skullcap. Devika hesitated, then placed her hand on her chest and nodded. He smiled and said, "Adaab, beti." Then a young woman doctor from the district hospital held out her hand. Devika shook it firmly.
Later, a very old man at the wedding stepped back when she began to bend. "No, no, namaste is enough," he said, hands folded. She folded hers too. Tejas laughed. "How do you know what to do?" Devika shrugged. "I don't. I just watch what they seem comfortable with." He noticed his grandmother nodding approvingly from the cot.

qa.q: How did Devika greet the young woman doctor?
qa.a: She shook her hand firmly.

qa.q: How did Devika feel arriving without a rule book, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little hesitant, but calm enough to watch each person and follow their comfort.

qa.q: Why is Devika's way of greeting polite?
qa.a: She reads each person's cue, their age, faith and comfort, rather than using one fixed rule, so everyone feels respected.

qa.q: How might Tejas's grandmother see Devika?
qa.a: She probably approves of Devika, pleased by the respect shown to her and to the others, as her nod suggests.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult choosing between touching feet, a handshake or namaste depending on each person's age, faith and comfort.

passage:
The whole lane calls me Irfan chacha, and I've lived opposite the Sharma family for thirty years. Last Diwali their son Sahil, twenty-four, back from his job in Hyderabad, came across to greet me. He started to bend down to touch my feet. We don't do that in my family, and I didn't want him to feel he had to. So I caught his shoulders gently and said, "No need, beta. Come, hug your chacha." He looked relieved, I think, and hugged me hard.
A moment later, Pandit Tripathi from the temple came by, and Sahil bent to him too. Panditji put his hand on the boy's head and blessed him loudly. Sahil beamed.
I watched him walk back home and thought: two different answers, both love. I only hope the boy felt we both saw him, not that we were testing whether he'd do it right.

qa.q: What did Irfan chacha say when Sahil bent down?
qa.a: "No need, beta. Come, hug your chacha."

qa.q: What was Irfan chacha feeling as he watched Sahil walk home?
qa.a: He felt warm and thoughtful, glad that both his hug and Panditji's blessing were love, and hopeful Sahil felt seen.

qa.q: What did both elders get right?
qa.a: Each responded warmly in their own way, one declining gently and one blessing, so Sahil felt welcomed rather than judged.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt when Irfan chacha stopped him and hugged him?
qa.a: Sahil seemed relieved and happy, hugging hard, perhaps glad he did not have to guess the right custom.

grounding: It illustrates an elder who notices a young person bend and gently declines, while another blesses warmly, both making him feel seen.

passage:
At the old-age home in Shillong, run by a church trust, nobody touched anyone's feet. It wasn't the custom there. Hrithik, twenty-five, from Varanasi, had grown up doing it for every elder, and in his first week as a care worker he felt strangely empty-handed. How was he supposed to show respect?
His colleague Devika, a local nurse, watched him fuss over it. "You'll see," she said.
So Hrithik did what he could. He learnt each resident's name and story. He sat with Mr Kharkongor every afternoon and listened to the same war stories, asking new questions each time. He brought Mrs Syiem her tea exactly as she liked it, weak, three sugars. When old Mr Lyngdoh couldn't sleep, Hrithik read to him. A month later, Mrs Syiem told Devika, "That boy respects us more than my own grandsons." Hrithik heard it from the corridor, and smiled.

qa.q: How does Mrs Syiem like her tea?
qa.a: Weak, with three sugars.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel in his first week at the home?
qa.a: He felt strangely empty-handed and unsure, not knowing how to show respect without touching feet.

qa.q: How did Hrithik show respect without the custom?
qa.a: Through care, time and listening: learning names and stories, sitting with residents, making tea just right and reading to someone who couldn't sleep.

qa.q: How does Mrs Syiem see Hrithik?
qa.a: She sees him as deeply respectful, even more than her own grandsons, because of his attention and care.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who respects elders through care, time and listening where feet-touching is not practised.

passage: It was Eid in Marseille, and the flat filled with aunties, uncles and cousins. They lifted Fatima, two, from arm to arm, fed her dates and pastry, and kissed her cheeks. She squealed and clapped. Then Uncle Diego, whom she didn't know, pinched her cheek hard. Fatima's lip wobbled. She ran and hid behind Maman's legs, peeking out. Later, when the doorbell rang again, she ran to the door, laughing.

qa.q: What did the relatives feed Fatima?
qa.a: Dates and pastry.

qa.q: How did Fatima feel when Uncle Diego pinched her cheek?
qa.a: She felt upset and startled, her lip wobbling, and hid behind Maman's legs.

qa.q: What could Maman do when a stranger pinches Fatima's cheek?
qa.a: Maman could let her hide safely and ask guests to wave or smile first instead of pinching.

qa.q: How might Uncle Diego feel when Fatima runs away?
qa.a: He may feel a little sad or embarrassed, as he probably meant it as affection.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler who enjoys the fuss of visiting relatives but hides when a stranger pinches her cheek.

passage: When Ishita aunty came to visit their Indore flat, Dadi said, "Madhav, atithi devo bhava. Guest is like God." Madhav, five, carried a glass of water with both hands. Aunty smiled and said, "Thank you, beta." Then Dadi put the last gulab jamun on aunty's plate. Madhav stared at it. He had wanted it all day. His lip went out a little. Aunty saw. She cut it in half and gave him one piece. Dadi laughed, "See? Serve with love, and love comes back." Madhav ate slowly, happy.

qa.q: What did Dadi put on Ishita aunty's plate?
qa.a: The last gulab jamun.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when the last gulab jamun went to aunty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, his lip going out a little, because he had wanted it all day.

qa.q: What did Madhav learn from the visit?
qa.a: That serving guests first is a way of showing love, and kindness often comes back.

qa.q: How might Ishita aunty have felt when she saw Madhav's face?
qa.a: She probably felt tender and amused, so she shared half the sweet with him.

grounding: It illustrates a child told atithi devo bhava who serves the guest and learns the best portion goes to the visitor first.
